claims.text: CrFeCoNiX alloys may be examined in single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states.
The identity of X as Si, Mn, or Al governs whether a stable, coherent protective oxide forms above 900 °C.
Al in CrFeCoNiAl forms high-melting, low-diffusivity Al2O3.
Si in CrFeCoNiSi forms high-melting, low-diffusivity SiO2.
Al2O3 or SiO2 will form a dense, adherent scale on the corresponding CrFeCoNiX alloy.
Mn forms volatile or poorly adherent Mn oxides in CrFeCoNiMn.
Mn-containing scales tend to crack or spall.
A coherent Al2O3 or SiO2 layer acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress.
Dense, thermodynamically stable Al- or Si-rich oxide limits oxygen diffusion and minimizes stress buildup.
Mn oxides undergo rapid growth because they have higher diffusivity and lower melting points.
Rapid growth of Mn oxides promotes cracking and spallation.
Under matched high-temperature oxidative conditions, Al-containing alloys will have more stable, coherent, adherent scales and lower spallation than Mn-containing alloys.
Si-containing alloys may behave similarly to Al-containing alloys.
The controlled comparison holds processing, microstructural state, exposure temperature, atmosphere, and duration constant while changing X.
CrFeCoNi without a reactive X element can serve as a baseline, with direct comparisons among Si-, Mn-, and Al-containing variants as an alternative baseline.
The proposed behavior is bounded to exposure above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres and may not persist at lower temperatures or in non-oxidative environments.
Microstructure, processing history, and oxygen partial pressure may alter oxide adherence and growth.
The hypothesis is falsified if changing X produces no significant scale differences, or if the Mn-containing alloy forms a scale as stable and adherent as the Al- or Si-containing alloys.
